subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 9 periods = 405 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 45min

periods.activity_title: Into the Space Station: First Reading and Pre-Reading Warm-Up

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.205): paired discussion on 'feathered friends' and pets in space.
Let us read (p.206): insert vowels to decode key vocabulary before reading.

time_bands.activity: Open with the pre-reading paired discussion from 'Let us read' (p.205): students talk briefly about feathered friends and whether a bird could accompany astronauts. Take two or three pairs' responses to the class.

Work through the vowel-insertion vocabulary task from 'Let us read' (p.206) together: write each consonant frame on the board and invite students to call out the missing vowels, then confirm meanings as a class.

Read the first half of the story aloud — teacher reads, students follow in their textbooks (p.205–210), pausing at natural scene breaks to ask a quick comprehension check question and clarify any unfamiliar phrasing.
Brief class share: ask two or three students to say in one sentence what they have found most surprising so far about Claribel's arrival on the space station.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading discussion works best when students are asked to justify their predictions — 'Why do you think that?' draws out richer reasoning than a simple yes/no. A common pitfall is rushing past the vowel-insertion task; the words (regulation, forbidden, dietitian) recur throughout the story and are worth securing now. Students who finish the vocabulary task early can try to use two of the words in a sentence about space travel.

periods.activity_title: Claribel in Crisis: Comprehension and Extract Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.209): four brief-answer questions on Sven's motive and Claribel's adaptation.
Let us discuss (p.211): true-or-false statements covering Parts I and II of the story.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.212): read Extract 1 on Sven's construction skills and answer all four questions independently.

time_bands.activity: Read the second half of the story aloud — teacher reads pp.210–213 while students follow — pausing at the moment Claribel is found unconscious and again at the air-purifier revelation.

Work through 'Let us discuss' (p.209) as a class discussion: students share answers to the four brief-answer questions on Sven's scientific curiosity and Claribel's behaviour in zero gravity, building a class consensus on each.
Students work individually on the true-or-false task from 'Let us discuss' (p.211), then pairs compare verdicts and agree on justifications drawn from the story text.
Whole-class check of the true-or-false verdicts; invite students to read the exact sentence from the text that confirms each answer.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the story's crisis and resolution aloud, students are ready to interrogate the details. Watch for the common confusion between the alarm that failed silently and the second circuit that was never connected — these are two distinct failures, and the true-or-false task surfaces both. The extract on Sven's construction skills (p.212) is rich but time-consuming; assigning it as self-directed reading tonight keeps class time focused on discussion.

periods.activity_title: Canaries and Miners: Critical Extract Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.213): Extract 2 — four questions on the air-crisis dialogue and figurative language.
Let us think and reflect (p.213): extended questions — purpose of alarm, crew's changing attitude towards Claribel.

time_bands.activity: Read Extract 2 ('Jim! There's something wrong with the air…') aloud together from p.213, with students reading the character lines in turns, so the dialogue's urgency comes through.

Work through all four questions on Extract 2 from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.213): the fill-in on the canary–miner reference, Jim's dismissal, the meaning of 'shook Jim,' and what passing the oxygen bottle 'like a pipe of peace' reveals — discussing each in whole class before moving on.

Students write a short response (four to five sentences) to the two extended questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.213) — the purpose of the alarm and how the crew's attitude to Claribel shifted — then two or three share their answers aloud.
Teacher poses the closing question: 'What does half a million dollars of engineering being defeated by a canary tell us about problem-solving?' Students give one-word answers as a class round-up.

periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the air-purifier crisis through the story, students can now work on the author's craft — figurative language ('pipe of peace') and irony (the failed duplicate alarm). The extended questions reward students who think across the whole story arc, so encourage them to name specific moments rather than generalise. Students who find the extended questions challenging can begin with a bullet-point plan before writing prose.

periods.activity_title: Monika and Toby: Critical Listening to an Alien Conversation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.217): listen and mark true or false against five statements about Monika and Toby.
Let us listen (p.218): listen again and fill in the blanks with exact words from the conversation.

time_bands.activity: Set the scene briefly: students read only the names 'Monika' and 'Toby' and the fact that Toby is a Martian stranded on Earth. Ask students to predict one thing Monika might want to know about him.

Read the Monika–Toby conversation (p.249 transcript) aloud with expression — teacher takes both voices, or two confident students are cast — while the class listens. Students then mark the five true-or-false statements from 'Let us listen' (p.217) individually.
Read the conversation a second time at a steady pace; students now fill in the five blanks from 'Let us listen' (p.218) with the exact words they hear.
Class check: call on individual students for each blank, then work through the true-or-false verdicts together, asking students to quote the line that proved each statement true or false.

Brief class reflection: in one sentence each, students compare Toby's alien abilities with Claribel's special sensitivity in the story — two very different 'outsiders' who surprise the humans around them.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript (p.249) is self-contained and needs no additional material. Watch for the common error on statement 5 — students often mishear 'with my eye closed' and conflate it with seeing clearly without eyes; a third short reading of that section can clarify. The connecting question in the closing band is informal and ungraded — its purpose is to keep the chapter's theme of unexpected allies alive.

periods.activity_title: Speak Up: Silent Letters and Giving Space-Science Advice

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.?): read story words aloud, circle silent letters; extend to ten more words.
Let us speak (p.?): pair work — ask for and give advice using two science-project situations.

time_bands.activity: Write the four words from the story (ballet, alarm, whistle, psychologist) on the board with their phonetic guides. Students say each aloud, circle the silent letters in their books, then work through the ten additional words (receipt, debris, pneumonia, island, wreck, aisle, almond, campaign, foreign, fasten), calling out silent letters as a group.

Students work in pairs on the two advice-giving situations from 'Let us speak': one partner needs help with a solar-system model for the Science Exhibition, the other needs a strategy for the Chandrayaan-3 quiz — then roles swap so everyone practises both asking and advising.
Two or three pairs perform their advice exchange for the class; after each, the audience names one strong phrase the advisor used and suggests one improvement to make the advice more specific.

periods.teacher_notes: Silent-letter rules in English are pattern-based but irregular, so the goal is recognition and confident reading aloud rather than memorisation of rules. In the advice-giving pairs, students sometimes default to listing commands rather than using advisory structures; write 'I feel you should…' and 'You should ensure…' on the board at the start of the pair-work phase as visible scaffolds. Students who are hesitant to speak before the class can share their best single piece of advice rather than the whole exchange.
materials: Board or chart with word list

periods.activity_title: The Importance of Internet: Planning, Drafting and Sharing an Article

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.?): complete the social-media web, then draft a full three-paragraph article on the importance of the internet.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the article format: show a model structure on the board — heading, writer's name, three paragraphs with their purposes. Briefly discuss what 'the importance of the internet' might include, collecting six to eight ideas from the class.

Students complete the social-media web from 'Let us write,' filling the spokes with internet uses; teacher circulates and prompts students who leave spokes blank to think of education, communication, entertainment or commerce.

Students draft their three-paragraph article — introduction, uses and examples, closing comment or quote — using the web as a plan; teacher models an opening sentence for Paragraph 1 on the board and then withdraws so students write independently.

Students swap articles with a partner, read once, and mark one strength and one suggestion for improvement before returning the draft; teacher asks two or three students to read their closing paragraph aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage often write a strong first paragraph and rush the third; remind them before they begin that the closing paragraph carries the reader's lasting impression. A common structural error is omitting the writer's name — point to the model format on the board. The peer-response phase is kept brief and focused on one positive and one suggestion; open-ended peer feedback at this stage tends to produce generic comments rather than useful revision notes.

periods.activity_title: Word Blends and Future Time: Vocabulary and Grammar in Focus

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.214): match eight adjectives (nagging, vague, etc.) to the correct nouns.
Let us learn (p.214): combine word pairs from two columns to form merged words; give meanings.
Let us learn (p.215): identify the time reference of 'will' in the given sentence from the story.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.216): fill eight blanks with the correct future-tense form (Simple Present, Present Progressive, will, going to).

time_bands.activity: Display the eight adjectives from 'Let us learn' (p.214) on the board. Students match each adjective to the correct noun in their books, then locate and underline the sentences in the story text that use each adjective — this grounds new vocabulary in the narrative.

Introduce merged words using the story's own example 'intercom' (internal + communication). Students combine the six word-pairs from the two columns in 'Let us learn' (p.214), write the merged word and a brief meaning, then compare with a partner.

Read the story sentence 'It will mean that you're being doubly safeguarded' aloud and discuss the question from 'Let us learn' (p.215): what time does 'will' refer to here? Build a brief reference table on the board showing the four ways English expresses future time (will, going to, Simple Present, Present Progressive) with one example each.

Students complete two or three of the eight fill-in-blank sentences from 'Let us learn' (p.216) in class as guided practice with the reference table visible; the remaining five sentences are set for independent work at home.

periods.teacher_notes: The adjective-matching task works well when students are required to return to the text — it re-reads the story purposefully and shows adjectives functioning in context rather than in isolation. A common confusion in the future-tense table is between 'going to' (planned intention) and 'will' (prediction or decision made at the moment of speaking); use the story's context to illustrate: the narrator decides at the moment of speaking to warn Jim, so 'will' fits there. The homework fill-in task extends the grammar practice across a wider set of contexts.
materials: Board for the future-tense reference table

periods.activity_title: Future Tense in Action: Grammar Consolidation and Application

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.217): fill six blanks in an AI-themed passage using the correct future-tense verb forms.

time_bands.activity: Brief recap of the four future-time forms from the previous unit on 'will,' 'going to,' Simple Present and Present Progressive — students call out one example of each from memory; teacher writes them on the board.

Students read the AI-themed passage from 'Let us learn' (p.217) silently, then fill all six blanks with the correct future-tense form of the verb in brackets; teacher circulates and prompts students who hesitate to check whether the context implies a fixed schedule, a prediction, or a plan.

Class review: call on six different students for the six answers; for each, ask the student to justify their choice by naming the time signal in the sentence (e.g., 'By 2040' signals a future prediction — 'will have' or 'will').

Students write two original sentences — one about the space station in the story using 'will' and one about their own life using 'going to' — to demonstrate they can apply the forms outside the passage context.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the reference table and the first set of fill-in sentences, students are ready to transfer the grammar to a longer, more varied passage. The AI-paragraph context is deliberately different from the story's setting, which tests genuine understanding rather than pattern-matching to familiar sentences. Watch for students who choose 'will' for every blank by default; the time-signal justification in the review phase reveals whether they are reasoning or guessing.
materials: Board with four future-tense forms from previous work

periods.activity_title: Feathered Guardians: Exploring Animals as Early-Warning Systems

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.?): read examples of animals sensing natural calamities and decide whether the claim is supported.
Let us explore (p.?): in groups of four, make a simple bird feeder using cardboard and chart paper.

time_bands.activity: Students read the 'Let us explore' examples of animals sensing calamities — elephants and flamingos before the 2004 tsunami, oxen and geese before the 1805 Naples quake, migratory birds dodging storms — and discuss in pairs whether the evidence convinces them, naming the strongest example.

Whole-class discussion: pairs share their verdict and the example they found most persuasive; teacher charts on the board the animal, the calamity and the behaviour observed, building a collective evidence map.

Groups of four make a simple bird feeder from the cardboard and chart paper provided, following the picture guide in 'Let us explore'; teacher circulates with quick structural checks to ensure the feeder can hold weight, and groups label their feeder with one fact about birds as environmental sentinels.

Each group holds up their bird feeder and reads out their label fact; the class votes on the most surprising fact, and the teacher connects the activity back to Claribel — the canary who proved that a small bird's sensitivity can outperform half a million dollars of engineering.

periods.teacher_notes: The animal-calamity reading connects the story's central idea — that low-tech biological sensitivity outperforms high-tech engineering — to real documented events, giving students evidence to evaluate rather than simply accept. Students sometimes treat the bird-feeder activity as craft rather than science; the labelling requirement and the closing connection to Claribel keep the interdisciplinary purpose in view. Groups that finish the feeder early can add a second fact about a bird species native to their region.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to a narrative text using comprehension, inference and critical analysis as the vehicles.
items.source_context: Sven's canary Claribel aboard a space station; air-purifier failure; canary-as-sentinel theme; figurative language in crisis dialogue.
items.item_stem:
Read the statements below and write True or False for each. Support each answer with a word or phrase from the story.
1. Sven smuggled Claribel aboard the space station without any stated purpose.
2. Claribel was found unconscious because the air purifier had frozen during an eclipse.
3. The narrator's decision to warn Jim was based on his knowledge of miners and canaries.
4. The crew revived Claribel using oxygen from the space station's main supply.

options.text: Claribel was found unconscious because the air purifier had frozen during an eclipse.
Sven smuggled Claribel aboard the space station without any stated purpose.
The crew revived Claribel using oxygen from the space station's main supply.
The narrator's decision to warn Jim was based on his knowledge of miners and canaries.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. False — Sven gave a scientific reason: he wanted to observe how a bird behaves in zero gravity. 2. True — the air purifier froze during a rare eclipse of Earth's shadow. 3. True — the narrator recalled the historical use of canaries in coal mines to detect gas. 4. False — the crew used oxygen from an emergency cylinder, not the main supply.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to a narrative text using comprehension, inference and critical analysis as the vehicles.
items.source_context: Sven's canary Claribel aboard a space station; air-purifier failure; canary-as-sentinel theme; figurative language in crisis dialogue.
items.item_stem: At the end of the story, the narrator wryly suggests that a visitor who hears an unexpected snatch of birdsong on a space station should feel 'doubly reassured' rather than alarmed. What does this closing remark reveal about the narrator's view of the relationship between low-tech and high-tech solutions? Use evidence from the story's events to support your answer.

expected_elements: Identifies the narrator's ironic or wry tone in the closing remark.
Notes that expensive engineering (the duplicate alarm) failed while the canary succeeded.
Argues that biological sensitivity can surpass mechanical systems in reliability.
Supports the point with a specific story event, such as the frozen air purifier or the disconnected alarm circuit.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a dialogue and demonstrates understanding by verifying statements and recalling exact words as the vehicles.
items.source_context: Monika and Toby conversation: Martian abilities, energy from Sun, one-eye vision, breakfast revelation.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between Monika and Toby. Then decide whether each statement below is True or False.
1. Toby misses his people and his home on his planet.
2. Martians eat ice cream and chocolates to get their energy.
3. Toby tells Monika that he saw a red toy car in her pocket.
4. Toby claims he can see through mountains, clouds, wood and metals.

options.text: Martians eat ice cream and chocolates to get their energy.
Toby claims he can see through mountains, clouds, wood and metals.
Toby misses his people and his home on his planet.
Toby tells Monika that he saw a red toy car in her pocket.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — Toby says 'I miss my people and home.' 2. False — Martians get their energy from the Sun; they do not eat. 3. False — Toby sees a blue aeroplane, not a red toy car. 4. True — Toby says he can see beyond mountains and clouds, wood and even metals.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a dialogue and demonstrates understanding by verifying statements and recalling exact words as the vehicles.
items.source_context: Monika and Toby conversation: Martian abilities, energy from Sun, one-eye vision, breakfast revelation.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation again. Fill in the blanks with the exact words from the conversation.
1. Monika says: "I am happy to have you as my _______________."
2. Toby says: "We get our energy from the _______________."
3. Toby says: "I can see that you are carrying a toy in your pocket. It's a _______________ aeroplane."
4. Monika says (with surprise): "_______________ my goodness!"

items.item_stem: Read the following sentence aloud to your teacher or partner: 'The astronaut used his wrench to fasten the panel, but the whistle of escaping air alarmed the whole crew.' Identify and name aloud every silent letter in the underlined words (wrench, fasten, whistle, alarmed).

expected_elements: Reads the sentence fluently without mispronouncing silent-letter words.
Correctly identifies: 'w' in wrench, 't' in fasten, 't' in whistle.
Confirms 'alarmed' has no silent letter, showing discriminating awareness.
Uses clear articulation and appropriate pace when reading aloud.

items.source_lo: Student reads aloud with attention to pronunciation and engages in guided conversation to ask for and give advice as the vehicles.
items.source_context: Silent letters in story vocabulary; advice-giving on a solar-system model and Chandrayaan-3 quiz preparation.
items.item_stem: Imagine a classmate is anxious about the school's inter-class science quiz on space exploration. In a role-play with your partner, ask your classmate what they are finding difficult and give them at least two specific pieces of advice, using phrases such as 'I feel you should…' and 'You should ensure…'. Your advice must be specific to the topic of space exploration.

expected_elements: Uses at least one advisory phrase (e.g., 'I feel you should…') correctly.
Gives two distinct, topic-specific pieces of advice about space exploration.
Listens to the partner's concern before offering advice; responds to it.
Maintains a supportive, appropriate register throughout the exchange.

items.item_stem: A school magazine has invited students to contribute a short article. Write the opening paragraph (introduction only) of an article titled 'The Importance of Internet.' Your introduction should state what the internet is and why it matters, in three to four clear sentences. Include your name as the writer below the title.

expected_elements: Includes heading 'The Importance of Internet' and writer's name.
Introduces the topic clearly in three to four sentences.
States what the internet is and at least one reason it matters.
Uses formal register appropriate for a school magazine article.

items.item_stem: Write a complete three-paragraph article titled 'The Importance of Internet' for your school magazine. Your article should include: a general introduction to the topic; a paragraph explaining at least three uses of the internet with specific examples; and a closing paragraph with a thoughtful comment or quote that leaves the reader with something to reflect on. Include the title and your name.

expected_elements: Three clearly demarcated paragraphs with heading and writer's name.
Introduction presents the internet as a transformative global tool.
Second paragraph names at least three distinct uses with concrete examples.
Closing paragraph ends with a memorable comment, reflection or apt quote.

items.source_context: Adjective–noun matching from story; merged words (blends); four forms of future time reference — will, going to, Simple Present, Present Progressive.
items.item_stem:
The story 'Feathered Friend' is set on a space station of the future. Read the sentences below about an imaginary future mission and fill in each blank with the correct future-tense form of the verb in brackets. Choose from: will, going to, Simple Present or Present Progressive, and be prepared to explain your choice.
1. The mission debrief __________ (begin) at 09:00 tomorrow — it is already in the schedule.
2. Scientists believe that space canaries __________ (play) a key role in future station safety.
3. Look — the air-alarm technician __________ (connect) the second circuit right now.
4. The crew has decided: they __________ (keep) Claribel on board permanently.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. begins (Simple Present for a fixed timetabled event) 2. will play (prediction about the future) 3. is connecting (Present Progressive for an action happening at this moment) 4. are going to keep (a decision already made).

items.item_stem: You have read about elephants, flamingos and migratory birds that appeared to sense natural calamities before they struck. Write a paragraph of five to six sentences explaining whether you find this evidence convincing. Name at least two of the animals and the specific events mentioned, and give one reason why scientists might be cautious about accepting this evidence.

expected_elements: Names at least two animals and their associated calamity events correctly.
States a clear personal verdict on whether the evidence is convincing.
Provides at least one reason why scientists might remain cautious.
Writes in connected prose with a clear opening and closing sentence.

items.source_context: Animals sensing natural calamities (tsunami, earthquake, storms); making a bird feeder; Claribel as living early-warning system.
items.item_stem: Design and build a bird feeder using cardboard, chart paper and any other classroom materials. On a label attached to your feeder, write: (a) the name of one bird species that might use it and one fact about that bird's role as a sentinel or indicator of environmental health; (b) one sentence connecting your feeder to the idea in 'Feathered Friend' that living creatures can protect humans.

expected_elements: Feeder is structurally sound and could realistically hold seed or food.
Label names a real local bird species and gives an accurate sentinel fact.
Connecting sentence links the feeder meaningfully to the story's theme.
Overall presentation shows care and reflects the conservation purpose.
